name: upperBound
title: Upper bound
informal_statement:
Let $(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{R}, T)$ be a  localised regularised Brascamp-Lieb datum, let  $\vec{\alpha} \in \R_{>0}^J$ and $\beta \in \R_{\geq 0}$. Assume $\mathcal{D}$ is $(\vec{\alpha}, \beta)$-perceptive and  $\mathrm{rk}_{\alpha_j}(\ell_j) = \dim H_j$ for each $j \in J$.
Then, writing $d = \dim H$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rlub}
\mathrm{BL}_{\mathbf{g}}(\mathcal{D}, \mathcal{R}, T)
\leq d^{\frac{\mathrm{Ac}(\mathcal{D})}{2}}  \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{D}) \prod_{j \in J} \alpha_j^{-q_j \dim H_j} N(\mathcal{D}, \mathcal{R}, T)^{\frac{\mathrm{Ac}(\mathcal{D})-d+\beta}{2}} \norm{T^{-1}}^{\frac{\beta}{2}}.
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{D}) = \prod_{j \in J} q_j^{-q_j  \dim H_j / 2}$ and $N(\mathcal{D}, \mathcal{R}, T) =  \norm{T + \sum_{j} q_j \ell^* R_j \ell_j}$.

    [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] {F : J → Type*} [(j : J) → NormedAddCommGroup (F j)]
    [(j : J) → InnerProductSpace ℝ (F j)] [(j : J) → FiniteDimensional ℝ (F j)]
    (hE : Module.finrank ℝ E ≠ 0)
    (D : locRegDatum E F) (α : J → NNReal) (β : NNReal) (hα : ∀ i, 0 < α i)
    (hP : D.IsMetricPercep α β)
    (hS : ∀ j : J, (D.map j).EssentialRank rfl (α j) = Module.finrank ℝ (F j)) :
    let M_max := (D.loc + ∑ j, (D.weight j) • (D.map j).adjoint ∘ₗ (D.reg j) ∘ₗ (D.map j))
    loc_reg_constant_g D ≤
      (Module.finrank ℝ E : NNReal)^(D.Acuity / 2 : ℝ) *
      (∏ j, (D.weight j)^(- (D.weight j : ℝ) * Module.finrank ℝ (F j) / 2)) *
      (∏ j, (α j)^(- (D.weight j : ℝ) * Module.finrank ℝ (F j))) *
      ‖M_max.toContinuousLinearMap‖₊^((D.Acuity.toReal - Module.finrank ℝ E + β) / 2) *

name: ae_tendsto_comp_of_ae_tendsto_of_forall_continuousAt
title: Continuous Mapping Theorem (almost sure convergence version)
informal_statement:
\leanok
  Let $(X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ be a net (indexed by a directed set $A$) of $\genspace$-valued
  random variables converging in probability to a random variable~$X$,
  $X_\alpha \tendsas X$ (along $A$).
  If $g \colon \genspaceA \to \genspaceB$ is a function which is continuous
  at every point of some Borel set $\genspaceA_0 \subseteq \genspaceA$ such that
  $\PR[X \in \genspaceA_0] = 1$,
  then $g(X_\alpha) \tendsas g(X)$ (along $A$).
informal_proof:
\chapter{The Continuous Mapping Theorem, Almost Sure Version}

This section contains a proof of the almost sure convergence version of the Continuous Mapping
Theorem (the simplest of three distinct statements by the same general name).
See \url{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_mapping_theorem} for more details.

Fix a probability space $(\PRspace,\PRsigma,\PR)$ once and for all (implicit
in the statements below).

Let $\genspaceA$ and $\genspaceB$ be two topological spaces,
equipped with their respective Borel sigma algebras.
%$\borelOf{\genspaceA}$ and $\borelOf{\genspaceB}$

\begin{theorem}[Continuous Mapping Theorem (almost sure convergence version)]
  \label{thm:cont_map_thm_as}
  \lean{ae_tendsto_comp_of_ae_tendsto_of_forall_continuousAt}
  \leanok
  Let $(X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ be a net (indexed by a directed set $A$) of $\genspace$-valued
  random variables converging in probability to a random variable~$X$,
  $X_\alpha \tendsas X$ (along $A$).
  If $g \colon \genspaceA \to \genspaceB$ is a function which is continuous
  at every point of some Borel set $\genspaceA_0 \subseteq \genspaceA$ such that
  $\PR[X \in \genspaceA_0] = 1$,
  then $g(X_\alpha) \tendsas g(X)$ (along $A$).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  \leanok

  Let $C$ be the event that $X_\alpha \to X$. By assumption, $\PR[C] = 1$.

  Let $S$ be the event that $X \in \genspaceA_0$. By assumption, $\PR[S] = 1$.

  Note that $\PR [C \cap S] = 1$. For any $\omega \in C \cap S$
  we have $X_\alpha(\omega) \to X(\omega) \in \genspaceA_0$. Since $g$
  is continuous at $X(\omega) \in \genspaceA_0$ by assumption, we get from this that
  $g\big(X_\alpha(\omega)\big) \to g\big(X(\omega)\big)$. It follows that
  $\PR\Big[ g\big(X_\alpha(\omega)\big) \to g\big(X(\omega) \Big] \ge \PR[C \cap S] = 1$,
  so $g(X_\alpha) \tendsas g(X)$.
\end{proof}

name: ProbabilityMeasure.tendsto_map_of_forall_continuousAt
title: Continuous Mapping Theorem (convergence in distribution version)
informal_statement:
\leanok
  Let $(\mu_n)_{n \in \N}$ be a sequence of Borel probability
  measures on $\genspaceA$ converging weakly to a Borel probability
  measure $\mu$, i.e., $\mu_n \tendsweakly \mu$.
  Let $g \colon \genspaceA \to \genspaceB$ be a measurable function.
  Assume that $g$ is continuous
  at every point of some Borel set $\genspaceA_0 \subseteq \genspaceA$ such that
  $\mu[X \in \genspaceA_0] = 1$.
  Then we have $g_* \mu_n \tendsweakly g_* \mu$, where
  $g_*$ denotes the push-forward of measures.
informal_proof:
\chapter{The Continuous Mapping Theorem, Convergence in Distribution Version}

This section contains a proof of the convergence in distribution version of the Continuous Mapping
Theorem.
See \url{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_mapping_theorem} and
Billingsley "Convergence of Probability Measures" (2nd ed), Theorem 2.7.

Let $\genspaceA$ and $\genspaceB$ be two metric spaces.
%, equipped with their respective Borel sigma algebras.
%$\borelOf{\genspaceA}$ and $\borelOf{\genspaceB}$

\begin{lemma}[Preimage closure lemma]
  \label{lem:subset_preimage_closure}
  \lean{inter_closure_preimage_ss_preimage_closure_of_forall_continuousAt}
  \leanok
  Let $g \colon \genspaceA \to \genspaceB$ be a measurable function
  and let $\genspace_0 \subseteq \genspaceA$ be a set such that $g$
  is continuous at every point of $\genspace_0$.
  Then for any set $B \subseteq \genspaceB$ we have
  \begin{align*}
    \genspaceA_0 \cap \closure{g^{-1}(B)} \subseteq g^{-1}(\closure{B}) .
  \end{align*}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
  % \uses{}
  \leanok
  Suppose $x \in \genspaceA_0 \cap \closure{g^{-1}(B)}$.
  Since $x \in \closure{g^{-1}(B)}$, there exists
  a sequence $(x_n)_{n \in \N}$ in $g^{-1}(B)$ such that
  $x_n \to x$ as $n \to \infty$.
  Since $x \in \genspaceA_0$, $g$ is continuous at $x$,
  and therefore $g(x_n) \to g(x)$ as $n \to \infty$.
  Since $g(x_n) \in B$ for all $n$, we have $g(x) \in \closure{B}$,
  and therefore $x \in g^{-1}(\closure{B})$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Continuous Mapping Theorem (convergence in distribution version)]
  \label{thm:cont_map_thm_law}
  \lean{ProbabilityMeasure.tendsto_map_of_forall_continuousAt}
  \leanok
  Let $(\mu_n)_{n \in \N}$ be a sequence of Borel probability
  measures on $\genspaceA$ converging weakly to a Borel probability
  measure $\mu$, i.e., $\mu_n \tendsweakly \mu$.
  Let $g \colon \genspaceA \to \genspaceB$ be a measurable function.
  Assume that $g$ is continuous
  at every point of some Borel set $\genspaceA_0 \subseteq \genspaceA$ such that
  $\mu[X \in \genspaceA_0] = 1$.
  Then we have $g_* \mu_n \tendsweakly g_* \mu$, where
  $g_*$ denotes the push-forward of measures.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
  \uses{lem:subset_preimage_closure}
  \leanok
  By the portmanteau theorem, it suffices to show that for
  any closed set $F \subseteq \genspaceB$ we have
  \begin{align*}
    \limsup_{n \to \infty} g_* \mu_n (F) \; \le \; g_* \mu (F) .
  \end{align*}
  Recall that push-forwards are defined so that, e.g.,
  $g_* \mu_n (F) = \mu_n (g^{-1} (F))$.

  Calculate, using the assumptions
  $\mu_n \tendsweakly \mu$ (with portmanteau characterization again)
  and $\mu[\genspaceA_0^{\mathrm{c}}] = 0$
  and Lemma~\ref{lem:subset_preimage_closure}:
  \begin{align*}
    & \limsup_{n \to \infty} \mu_n [g^{-1} (F)] \\
    \le \; & \limsup_{n \to \infty} \mu_n \big[ \closure{g^{-1} (F)} \big] \\
    \le \; & \mu \big[ \closure{g^{-1} (F)} \big] \\
    %\overset{\text{L \ref{lem:subset_preimage_closure}}}{\le} \;
    = \;
      & \mu \big[ \genspaceA_0 \cap \closure{g^{-1} (F)} \big] \\
    \le \; & \mu \big[ g^{-1} (\closure{F}) \big]
  \end{align*}
  If $F \subseteq \genspaceB$ is closed then
  the last expression is
  $\mu \big[ g^{-1} (\closure{F}) \big] = g_* \mu (F)$,
  and the proof is thus complete.
\end{proof}

See \url{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kraft%E2%80%93McMillan_inequality} for more details.

Let $\sigma$ be a finite nonempty set, which we call the \emph{alphabet}.
We write $D = |\sigma|$ for the size of the alphabet.

\begin{definition}[Code]
  \label{def:Code}
  \lean{Code}
  \leanok
  A \emph{code} $C$ over the alphabet $\sigma$ is a finite set of finite strings
  over $\sigma$. The elements of $C$ are called \emph{codewords}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Unique decodability]
  \label{def:Unique_Decodability}
  \lean{UniquelyDecodable}
  \uses{def:Code}
  \leanok
  A code $C$ is \emph{uniquely decodable} if whenever two sequences of
  codewords $w_1 \cdots w_m = w_1' \cdots w_{m'}'$ produce the same
  concatenated string, the sequences are identical (in particular, $m = m'$
  and $w_i = w_i'$ for all $i$).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Kraft sum]
  \label{def:Kraft_Sum}
  \lean{kraftSum}
  \uses{def:Code}
  \leanok
  The \emph{Kraft sum} of a code $C$ over an alphabet of size $D$ is
  \[
    K(C) = \sum_{w \in C} D^{-|w|},
  \]
  where $|w|$ denotes the length of the codeword $w$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Tuple counting bound]
  \label{lem:count-tuples}
  \lean{count_tuples_le}
  \uses{def:Code, def:Unique_Decodability}
  \leanok
  Let $C$ be a uniquely decodable code and let $n, k$ be natural numbers.
  The number of $n$-tuples $(w_1, \ldots, w_n) \in C^n$ whose total length
  $|w_1| + \cdots + |w_n|$ equals $k$ is at most $D^k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
  \leanok
  Since $C$ is uniquely decodable, concatenation is injective on $n$-tuples:
  distinct $n$-tuples produce distinct strings.
  If the total length equals $k$, then the concatenation is a string
  of length $k$ over $\sigma$, and there are exactly $D^k$ such strings.
  Since distinct tuples map to distinct strings, the number of tuples is
  at most $D^k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Kraft sum power bound]
  \label{lem:kraft-pow}
  \lean{kraftSum_pow_le}
  \uses{def:Code, def:Unique_Decodability, def:Kraft_Sum}
  \leanok
  Let $C$ be a uniquely decodable code with a maximum codeword length
  $L = \max_{w \in C} |w|$.
  For all $n \geq 1$,
  \[
    K(C)^n \leq nL + 1.
  \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
  \uses{lem:count-tuples}
  \leanok
  Write $K = K(C)$.
  Expanding the $n$-th power using the multinomial expansion gives
  \[
    K^n
    = \biggl(\sum_{w \in C} D^{-|w|}\biggr)^{\!n}
    = \sum_{t \in C^n} \prod_{i=1}^{n} D^{-|t_i|}
    = \sum_{t \in C^n} D^{-\ell(t)},
  \]
  where $\ell(t) = |t_1| + \cdots + |t_n|$ is the total length of the
  $n$-tuple $t = (t_1, \ldots, t_n)$.

  Since each codeword has length at most $L$, the total length satisfies
  $0 \leq \ell(t) \leq nL$.
  Grouping tuples by their total length, we obtain
  \[
    K^n = \sum_{k=0}^{nL} A(n,k) \cdot D^{-k},
  \]
  where $A(n,k) = |\{t \in C^n : \ell(t) = k\}|$.

  By Lemma~\ref{lem:count-tuples}, $A(n,k) \leq D^k$, so each summand satisfies
  \[
    A(n,k) \cdot D^{-k} \leq D^k \cdot D^{-k} = 1.
  \]
  Since $k$ ranges over $\{0, 1, \ldots, nL\}$, there are $nL + 1$ summands, giving
  \[
    K^n \leq \sum_{k=0}^{nL} 1 = nL + 1.
  \]
\end{proof}

We also need the following classical inequality.

\begin{lemma}[Bernoulli's inequality]
  \label{lem:bernoulli}
  \lean{bernoulli_ineq}
  \leanok
  For all $a \geq 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
  \[
    (1 + a)^n \geq 1 + na.
  \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
  \leanok
  By induction on $n$. The base case $n = 0$ is immediate.
  For the inductive step, assume that $(1+a)^n \geq 1 + na$. Then
  \[
    (1+a)^{n+1}
    = (1+a)^n \cdot (1+a)
    \geq (1 + na)(1 + a)
    = 1 + (n+1)a + na^2
    \geq 1 + (n+1)a.
  \]
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[McMillan]
  \label{thm:mcmillan}
  \lean{mcmillan}
  \uses{def:Code, def:Unique_Decodability, def:Kraft_Sum}
  \leanok
  Every uniquely decodable code $C$ satisfies the Kraft inequality:
  \[
    K(C) \leq 1.
  \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  \uses{lem:kraft-pow, lem:bernoulli}
  \leanok
  Suppose for contradiction that $K = K(C) > 1$.
  Set $a = K - 1 > 0$ and $L = \max_{w \in C} |w|$.

  \medskip\noindent\textbf{Upper bound.}
  By Lemma~\ref{lem:kraft-pow}, for every $n \geq 1$,
  \[
    K^n \leq nL + 1.
  \]

  \medskip\noindent\textbf{Lower bound.}
  Since $K = 1 + a$, Bernoulli's inequality (Lemma~\ref{lem:bernoulli}) gives
  $K^N \geq 1 + Na$ for every $N \in \mathbb{N}$.
  Squaring, we obtain
  \[
    K^{2N} = (K^N)^2 \geq (1 + Na)^2 = 1 + 2Na + N^2 a^2 \geq 1 + N^2 a^2.
  \]

  \medskip\noindent\textbf{Contradiction.}
  Combining the upper and lower bounds for $n = 2N$:
  \[
    1 + N^2 a^2 \leq K^{2N} \leq 2NL + 1,
  \]
  which gives $N^2 a^2 \leq 2NL$, and hence $Na^2 \leq 2L$ for every $N \geq 1$.

  Since $a > 0$, we have $a^2 > 0$.
  By the Archimedean property, there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ with
  $Na^2 > 2L$, contradicting $Na^2 \leq 2L$.
  Therefore $K \leq 1$.
\end{proof}

    kraftSum C ≤ 1 := by sorry

name: SchauderFixedPointTheorem
title: Schauder fixed-point theorem
informal_statement:
If $C$ is a nonempty convex compact subset of a locally
convex Hausdorff topological vector space $E$ over $\mathbb{R}$, and $f : E \to E$ is continuous with
$f(C) \subseteq C$, then $f$ has a fixed point in $C$. -/
informal_proof:
\chapter{Schauder fixed-point theorem}

This section contains a proof of Schauder's fixed-point theorem.
See \url{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schauder_fixed-point_theorem} for more details.

\begin{theorem}
  \label{thm:SchauderFixedPointTheorem}
  \lean{SchauderFixedPointTheorem}
  If $C$ is a nonempty convex compact subset of a locally
convex Hausdorff topological vector space $E$ over $\mathbb{R}$, and $f : E \to E$ is continuous with
$f(C) \subseteq C$, then $f$ has a fixed point in $C$. -/
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
  For any $\epsilon > 0$, notice that the family of open sets
  $\{B_{\epsilon}(x) : x \in C\}$
  is an open covering of $C$. Because $C$ is compact, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $x_1, \dots, x_n \in C$ such that $K$ is covered by $B_{\epsilon}(x_i)$, $i = 1, \dots, n$.
  For each $i$, define $g_i(x)$ to be
  $\epsilon - ||x - x_i||$ if $||x - x_i|| \leq \epsilon$, else $0$.
  Then each $g_i$ is continuous, $g_i(x) \geq 0$, and $\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x)> 0$ for every $x \in C$.
  We define a function
  $g(x) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x) x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x)}$.
  $g$ is then a continuous function from $C$ to the convex hull $C_0$ of $x_1, \dots, x_n$.
  Also we can see that for any $x \in C$, $||g(x)-x|| \leq \epsilon$.
  Define $B := g \circ f$. $\tilde{B} := B | C_0$ is a continuous function $C_0 \to C_0$.
  Since $C_0$ is a compact convex subset of a finite dimensional vector space,
  we can apply the Brouwer fixed point theorem to get $z \in C_0$ such that $\tilde{B} = z$.
  Therefore, $g(f(z))=z$ and so
  $||f(z)-z|| = ||f(z) - g(f(x))|| \leq \epsilon$.

  Summarizing, for each $\epsilon > 0$ there exists $z \in C$ such that $||f(z) - z|| \leq \epsilon$.

  By compactness, there exists a strictly increasing sequence $m_k \in \mathbb{N}$, $k = 1, 2, \dots$, and a sequence $z_k \in C$ such that
  $||f(z_k)-z_k|| \leq 1/m_k$ and $f(z_k) \to x_0$ for some $x_0 \in C$.
  Then $z_k \to x_0$.
  As $f$ is continuous, $f(z_k) \to f(x_0)$. Therefore, $f(x_0)=x_0$.
\end{proof}

name: von_staudt_clausen
title: Von Staudt-Clausen Theorem
informal_statement:
For any positive integer $n$, the Bernoulli number $B_{2n}$ can be expressed as
    $B_{2n} = I_n - \sum_{(p-1)|2n} \frac{1}{p}$
    where $I_n$ is an integer and the sum is over all prime numbers $p$ such that $p-1$ divides $2n$. This is equivalent to saying that $B_{2n} + \sum_{(p-1)|2n} \frac{1}{p}$ is an integer.

    (fun j => (j + 1).Prime) , if j ∣ (2 * n) then (1 : ℚ) / (j+1) else 0) := by sorry
